stem: Why do different persons have different notions of development? Which of the following explanations is more important and why? (a) Because people are different. (b) Because life situations of persons are different.
solution:
**(b) Because life situations of persons are different** is the more important explanation.

1. Each person seeks the things that are **most important for them**, that is, the things that can fulfil their own aspirations, and what those things are is decided by the situation the person lives in.
2. Table 1.1 shows this directly. Landless rural labourers want more days of work and better wages and a local school able to provide quality education; prosperous farmers from Punjab want higher support prices and cheap labourers; a girl from a rich urban family wants as much freedom as her brother.
3. If people merely differed as individuals, persons in the same situation would still want quite different things. In practice they want much the same things, which shows that it is the **life situation**, and not personal difference alone, that shapes a person's notion of development.
groundedIn: § What Development Promises; § Different People, Different Goals; Table 1.1 — the chapter's table of developmental goals of different categories of persons, and its statement that each one seeks the things that are most important for them

stem: Do the following two statements mean the same? Justify your answer. (a) People have different developmental goals. (b) People have conflicting developmental goals.
solution:
**No, the two statements do not mean the same thing.**

1. **Different goals** means people seek different things. A prosperous farmer wants higher support prices while an urban unemployed youth wants a job; both goals can be met at the same time and neither harms the other.
2. **Conflicting goals** means one person's goal can be met only by defeating another's. Industrialists may want more dams for more electricity, but a dam submerges land and disrupts the lives of the tribals who are displaced, and they may prefer small check dams or tanks. A girl expects as much freedom and opportunity as her brother and expects him to share the household work; her brother may not like this.
3. So every conflicting goal is a different goal, but **not every different goal is conflicting**. What may be development for one may not be development for the other, and it may even be destructive for the other.
groundedIn: § What Development Promises; § Different People, Different Goals — the dam and displacement example, the brother and sister example, and the chapter's conclusion that what may be development for one may even be destructive for the other

stem: Give some examples where factors other than income are important aspects of our lives.
solution:
Besides income, people seek **equal treatment, freedom, security and the respect of others**, and they resent discrimination.

1. **Job security.** A job may give less pay but offer regular employment that enhances a person's sense of security, while another may offer high pay with no job security and leave no time for the family.
2. **Working conditions and family life.** Before accepting a job in a far off place a person weighs facilities for the family, the working atmosphere and the opportunity to learn.
3. **Dignity and respect for women.** Where women are engaged in paid work their dignity in the household and in society increases, and where there is respect for women there is more sharing of housework.
4. **A safe and secure environment**, which allows more women to take up a variety of jobs or to run a business.
5. **Friendship**, which cannot be measured and yet means a great deal to our lives.
groundedIn: § Income and Other Goals — people also seek equal treatment, freedom, security and respect of others, and the chapter's examples of a job with security against a job with high pay, and of respect for women

stem: Explain some of the important ideas of the above section in your own words.
solution:
The section makes four main points.

1. **Different persons can have different developmental goals**, because each seeks what is most important for their own life situation.
2. **What is development for one may not be development for another**, and it may even be destructive for the other, as a dam that brings electricity to some submerges the land of others.
3. **Income is a common goal but not the only one.** What people in Table 1.1 desire is regular work, better wages and a decent price for their produce; but they also seek equal treatment, freedom, security and the respect of others.
4. **People look at a mix of goals.** Money and the material things it buys are one factor on which life depends, but the quality of life also depends on non-material things. Many of these are not easily measured, and it would be wrong to conclude that what cannot be measured is not important.
groundedIn: § What Development Promises; § Income and Other Goals; Table 1.1 — different persons having different and even conflicting goals, and the conclusion that developmental goals are not only about better income but also about other important things in life

stem: Look at the picture printed beside this question, which shows a cluster of small huts crowded at the foot of a tall multi-storeyed apartment block. What should be the developmental goals for such an area?
solution:
The goal for such an area must be to **close the gap between the two kinds of living shown in the picture**.

1. **Regular work and better wages**, so that the families living in the huts earn enough to house and feed themselves decently.
2. **Proper housing with basic facilities**, in place of huts put up on open ground beside the flats.
3. **Public facilities provided collectively** - a local school able to provide quality education, basic health care, safe water and sanitation - because these are exactly the things that money in a poor household's pocket cannot buy for itself, and the cheapest way to have them is to provide them for everybody together.
4. **An end to social discrimination**, so that the people of the settlement take part in the life of the locality on equal terms.

A tall block of flats standing over a row of huts shows that the average prosperity of an area can hide sharp inequality, so the goal is not more building alone but a fairer share in what is built.
groundedIn: § What Development Promises; § Public Facilities; Table 1.1 — the developmental goals the chapter lists for landless rural labourers, and its argument that for many important things the best and cheapest way is to provide them collectively

context:
Read this newspaper report and answer the questions that follow:

A vessel dumped 500 tonnes of liquid toxic wastes into open-air dumps in a city and in the surrounding sea. This happened in a city called Abidjan in Ivory Coast, a country in Africa. The fumes from the highly toxic waste caused nausea, skin rashes, fainting, diarrhoea etc. After a month seven persons were dead, twenty in hospital and twenty six thousand treated for symptoms of poisoning.

A multinational company dealing in petroleum and metals had contracted a local company of the Ivory Coast to dispose the toxic waste from its ship.
stem: Who are the people who benefited and who did not?
solution:
**Who benefited:**

1. The **multinational company** dealing in petroleum and metals, which got the toxic waste taken off its ship cheaply instead of paying for safe disposal.
2. The **local company of the Ivory Coast**, which earned the money paid for the disposal contract.

**Who did not benefit:**

1. The **people of Abidjan**. Seven persons were dead within a month, twenty were in hospital and twenty six thousand were treated for symptoms of poisoning.
2. Everyone who depends on the city's air and on the surrounding sea, into which 500 tonnes of liquid toxic waste were dumped.

The case is an example of the chapter's own rule: what is development, or profit, for one may not be development for the other, and it may even be **destructive** for the other.
groundedIn: § What Development Promises; § Different People, Different Goals — the chapter's rule that what may be development for one may not be development for the other and may even be destructive for the other

context:
Read this newspaper report and answer the questions that follow:

A vessel dumped 500 tonnes of liquid toxic wastes into open-air dumps in a city and in the surrounding sea. This happened in a city called Abidjan in Ivory Coast, a country in Africa. The fumes from the highly toxic waste caused nausea, skin rashes, fainting, diarrhoea etc. After a month seven persons were dead, twenty in hospital and twenty six thousand treated for symptoms of poisoning.

A multinational company dealing in petroleum and metals had contracted a local company of the Ivory Coast to dispose the toxic waste from its ship.
stem: What should be the developmental goal for this country?
solution:
The developmental goal for the Ivory Coast should be **income and employment that do not cost its own people their health and their environment**.

1. **Protection of the health of citizens and of the environment**, with a firm bar on importing and dumping hazardous waste.
2. **Earnings from safe activity**, not from contracts to dispose of other countries' toxic waste.
3. **Public facilities**, in particular health care able to deal with an emergency of this kind and a clean and safe environment, which no individual can buy for himself.
4. Judged by the chapter's own test - whether an idea would benefit a large number of people or only a small group - this contract benefited one company and harmed twenty six thousand people, so it fails that test. A fair and just path for all is the goal such a country needs.
groundedIn: § National Development — the chapter's questions of what would be a fair and just path for all and whether an idea would benefit a large number of people or only a small group

stem: What can be some of the developmental goals for your village, town or locality?
solution:
Goals differ from one locality to another; for a typical village or small town they would include:

1. **More days of work and better wages** for labourers, and a decent price for the crops and other products people produce.
2. **A local school able to provide quality education**, so that children need not be sent elsewhere to study.
3. **Basic health facilities**, since a low infant mortality rate follows from adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities rather than from higher income alone.
4. **Collective provision of what people cannot buy separately** - safe drinking water, sanitation, security for the whole locality and a Public Distribution System that actually works.
5. **No social discrimination**, and the same freedom and opportunity for girls as for boys.

Different persons in the same locality will still rank these differently, so the fair test is whether a goal benefits a large number of people or only a small group.
groundedIn: § What Development Promises; § Public Facilities; Table 1.1 — the goals the chapter lists for landless rural labourers, and Kerala's adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities as the reason for its low infant mortality rate

subtopic: How to Compare Different Countries or States
stem: Give three examples where an average is used for comparing situations.
solution:
1. **Average income, or per capita income, of a country.** Since countries have different populations, total income cannot show what an average person earns, so the total income is divided by the total population and the averages are compared.
2. **Per capita income of states.** Table 1.3 compares Haryana at Rs 2,36,147, Kerala at Rs 2,04,105 and Bihar at Rs 40,982 for 2018-19.
3. **Infant Mortality Rate.** It is the number of children who die before the age of one year for every 1,000 live births in that year, and Table 1.4 uses it to compare Haryana at 30, Kerala at 7 and Bihar at 32.

Literacy rate, net attendance ratio, life expectancy at birth and mean years of schooling are averages used in the same way.
groundedIn: § How to Compare Different Countries; Table 1.3; Table 1.4 — average income as the total income of the country divided by its total population, the per capita income of select states, and the infant mortality rate and literacy rate used to compare Haryana, Kerala and Bihar

subtopic: How to Compare Different Countries or States
stem: Why do you think average income is an important criterion for development? Explain.
solution:
**Average income is important because it makes countries of different sizes comparable, and because income buys many of the things people need.**

1. For comparing countries, income is considered one of the **most important attributes**, on the understanding that more income means more of all the things human beings need. Whatever people like, and should have, they will be able to get with greater income.
2. Total income cannot be used for the comparison, because countries have different populations and a total will not tell us what an average person is likely to earn. Dividing total income by total population gives the **per capita income**, which can be compared.
3. The World Bank uses exactly this criterion in its World Development Reports to classify countries as high income, low middle income or low-income.
4. It remains only one criterion, since an average cannot show how that income is distributed.
groundedIn: § How to Compare Different Countries; § Average Income — income being considered one of the most important attributes for comparing countries, and the average income being used because countries have different populations

subtopic: How to Compare Different Countries or States
stem: Besides size of per capita income, what other property of income is important in comparing two or more societies?
solution:
The other important property is the **distribution of that income**, that is, how equitably it is shared among the people.

1. An average is useful for comparison but does not tell us how the income is distributed.
2. Table 1.2 makes the point. Country A and country B have five citizens each and the **same average income of Rs 10,000** a month, yet in country A the five earn between Rs 9,500 and Rs 10,500 while in country B four earn Rs 500 each and one earns Rs 48,000.
3. Country A is preferred because it has a **more equitable distribution**: there people are neither very rich nor extremely poor, whereas in country B most citizens are poor and one person is extremely rich.
groundedIn: § While averages are useful for comparison, they also hide disparities; Table 1.2 — two countries with identical average income where country A is preferred because it has more equitable distribution

subtopic: How to Compare Different Countries or States
stem: Suppose records show that the average income in a country has been increasing over a period of time. From this, can we conclude that all sections of the economy have become better? Illustrate your answer with an example.
solution:
**No, we cannot conclude that.**

1. A rise in the average income only tells us that the **total** income has grown faster than the population. It says nothing about who received the increase.
2. The whole increase can go to a few people while the rest stay where they were, and the average will still rise.
3. Take country B of Table 1.2, where four citizens earn Rs 500 a month and the fifth earns Rs 48,000. If the rich citizen's income rose to Rs 98,000 while the other four stayed at Rs 500, the average income would jump from Rs 10,000 to Rs 20,000 a month, yet four of the five citizens would be exactly as poor as before.
4. So a rising average has to be read together with the **distribution** of income before any claim is made about all sections of the economy.
groundedIn: § While averages are useful for comparison, they also hide disparities; Table 1.2 — in country B four citizens earn Rs 500 each and one earns Rs 48,000, yet its average income equals country A's, which is the chapter's demonstration that an average hides how income is distributed

subtopic: How to Compare Different Countries or States
stem: From the text, find out the per capita income level of about 10-15 low-income countries as per World Development Reports.
solution:
In the World Development Reports, a **low-income country is one with a per capita income of US$ 2500 per annum or less**, taking 2019 figures.

1. At the other end, countries with a per capita income of **US$ 49,300 per annum and above** in 2019 are called high income or rich countries, and these, excluding the countries of the Middle East and certain other small countries, are generally called developed countries.
2. India, with a per capita income of **US$ 6700** per annum in 2019, does not fall in either group; it comes in the **low middle income** category.
3. The chapter's text gives the cut-off and India's own figure but does not print the figures for individual low-income countries, so the 10-15 country figures have to be read off the World Development Report itself.
groundedIn: § How to Compare Different Countries — the World Development Reports classification, with US$ 49,300 and above as high income, US$ 2500 or less as low income, and India at US$ 6700 in 2019 in the low middle income category

stem: Write a paragraph on your notion of what should India do, or achieve, to become a developed country.
solution:
**India should raise the incomes of its people and, at the same time, give every citizen the health, education and public facilities that income alone cannot buy.** This is one defensible view among several.

1. **Raise incomes and spread them more evenly.** A higher per capita income matters, since more income does buy more of what people need, but it must not be an average that hides four poor citizens behind one rich one.
2. **Bring health and education up to the level of the best states.** Kerala shows what is possible: an infant mortality rate of 7 against Haryana's 30, and a net attendance ratio of 83 against 61, achieved with a lower per capita income.
3. **Provide the important things collectively** - schools, basic health care, a working Public Distribution System and a clean and safe environment - because that is both the best and the cheapest way to make them available to all.
4. **Lift India's human development rank.** India stood 132nd in the world in 2021-22, behind Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, and behind Nepal and Bangladesh in life expectancy despite a higher income than theirs.
5. **Keep the development sustainable**, so that this level can be maintained for future generations.

The test at every step is the chapter's own: would the idea benefit a large number of people, or only a small group?
groundedIn: § National Development; § Income and Other Criteria; Table 1.6 — the chapter's test of whether an idea would benefit a large number of people or only a small group, and India's human development position beside that of its neighbours

stem: Look at data in Tables 1.3 and 1.4. Is Haryana ahead of Kerala in literacy rate etc., as it is in terms of per capita income?
solution:
**No. Haryana leads Kerala in per capita income but falls behind it on every other measure.**

| Measure | Haryana | Kerala |
|---|---|---|
| Per capita income, 2018-19 | Rs 2,36,147 | Rs 2,04,105 |
| Infant Mortality Rate per 1,000 live births, 2018 | 30 | 7 |
| Literacy rate, 2017-18 | 82 per cent | 94 per cent |
| Net Attendance Ratio, secondary stage, 2017-18 | 61 | 83 |

1. In Kerala only 7 of every 1,000 children born die before completing one year, while in Haryana the figure is 30, nearly **three times** more.
2. Kerala is ahead of Haryana in literacy rate and in net attendance ratio as well.
3. The reason is that money in a person's pocket cannot buy all the goods and services needed to live well; Kerala has an adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities, and Haryana does not.
groundedIn: § Income and Other Criteria; § Public Facilities; Table 1.3; Table 1.4 — Haryana's higher per capita income beside Kerala's lower infant mortality rate and higher literacy rate and net attendance ratio, and the chapter's explanation that Kerala has adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities

stem: Think of other examples where collective provision of goods and services is cheaper than individual provision.
solution:
For many of the important things in life the best and also the cheapest way is to provide the goods and services **collectively**.

1. **Security for a locality.** Collective security for the whole locality costs far less than each house keeping its own security staff.
2. **Schools.** A government school serving all the children of a village costs a family far less than sending one child to a private school elsewhere, and a child can study only because many other children also want to study.
3. **Prevention of infectious disease.** Money cannot protect a person from infectious diseases unless the whole community takes preventive steps together.
4. **A clean environment.** A pollution-free environment and unadulterated medicines cannot be bought by an individual, however rich, unless the community as a whole has them.
5. **The Public Distribution System.** Where the PDS functions well the health and nutritional status of the people of that state is likely to be better.
groundedIn: § Public Facilities — collective security for the whole locality being cheaper than each house having its own security staff, the child who can study because many others also want to study, and preventive steps that only the whole community can take against infectious diseases

stem: Does availability of good health and educational facilities depend only on amount of money spent by the government on these facilities? What other factors could be relevant?
solution:
**No. The money spent matters, but it is not the only thing that decides whether the facilities are actually available.**

Other relevant factors:

1. **How well the service functions.** In some states the Public Distribution System functions well, and the health and nutritional status of the people of such states is certainly likely to be better. The same money can be spent well or badly.
2. **Whether the facility has been provided at all, and where.** Even now, in many areas children, and particularly girls, cannot go to high school because the government or society has not provided adequate facilities within reach.
3. **The provision already in place.** Kerala's low infant mortality rate follows from its adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities, built up over a long period rather than in one year's spending.
4. **What the community itself wants.** A child is able to study because many other children also want to study, and because many people believe that the government should open schools.
5. **Attitudes towards girls' education**, which decide whether the facilities that exist are used.
groundedIn: § Public Facilities — Kerala's adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities, the Public Distribution System functioning well in some states, and girls in many areas not being able to go to high school because the government or society has not provided adequate facilities

stem: In a study, it was found that in Tamil Nadu, 90 per cent of the people living in rural areas used a ration shop, whereas in West Bengal only 35 per cent of rural people did so. Where would people did better off and why?
solution:
**People in Tamil Nadu would be better off.**

1. A ration shop is the outlet of the **Public Distribution System**, so a figure of 90 per cent means the PDS reaches almost every rural household in Tamil Nadu, while in West Bengal, at 35 per cent, it reaches barely a third.
2. Where the Public Distribution System functions well, the **health and nutritional status** of the people of that state is certainly likely to be better.
3. Food grains bought at a ration shop cost less than in the open market, so a poor household in Tamil Nadu is able to eat adequately on the same income.
4. This is an example of the wider point that for many of the important things in life the best and the cheapest way is to provide them **collectively**, and that money in a person's pocket cannot by itself buy all the goods and services needed to live well.
groundedIn: § Public Facilities — in some states the Public Distribution System functions well and the health and nutritional status of the people of such states is certainly likely to be better
